claims.text: The target material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Processed bulk HfNbTaTiZr contains inherent microstructural defects and lattice disorder.
Pristine and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen-containing variants of the alloy are both within the proposed initial sample set.
Temperature-dependent correction factors for thermal expansion, defect-density changes, and quantum effects can be derived from in situ XRD and TEM over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Quantum effects and defect freeze-out dominate conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr at 0–200 K.
Thermal activation and oxygen-induced defect dynamics are significant for conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr at 300–1200 K.
Temperature causes lattice expansion and the formation or evolution of oxygen-related defect complexes in the alloy.
Oxygen-vacancy pairs are an example of the relevant defect complexes in oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
Lattice expansion and oxygen-related defects alter electron mean free paths and scattering rates.
Thermal expansion and defect evolution modify the electron-scattering environment and conduction pathways.
Incorporating empirically quantified microstructural changes into a conduction model compensates for errors caused by perfect-crystal assumptions.
The modified model will predict conductivity within 5% of experiment throughout both 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The oxygen-containing alloy has lower cryogenic conductivity because of defect-induced scattering and limited carrier activation.
Conductivity recovers or rises at high temperature because thermal activation compensates for scattering.
Conventional analytical models use defect-free, static-lattice assumptions and omit temperature-dependent microstructural evolution.
The model is applicable only to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K and to samples with oxygen content near 1 wt.% without further calibration.
Conductivity, lattice parameters, and defect concentration can be measured simultaneously or under matched conditions at 900 K.
A conductivity prediction error greater than 7% at 900 K falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The performance claim requires errors no greater than 5%, but the experiment falsifies it only above 7%. An error between 5% and 7% would violate the claimed outcome without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
The model is said to be calibrated and validated over the full 300–1200 K regime, which includes 900 K, so the proposed 900 K benchmark is not explicitly held out from calibration.
